approachQuestion.prompt:
Independent work groups. An undirected graph describes which workers can exchange a message directly. Return the number of groups in which every pair can communicate through zero or more links. Isolated workers each form a group.

Input: read-only adjacency lists for vertices 0 through V-1. Each edge appears in both endpoint lists, with no duplicates or self-loops. 1 <= V <= 200000; 0 <= E <= 400000. Output: one integer.

Example 1: lists=[[1],[0],[],[4],[3]], output=3: {0,1}, {2}, {3,4}.
Example 2: lists=[[],[],[]], output=3.

options.text: Scan every vertex. Whenever an unvisited vertex is found, increment the count and mark its entire reachable group with an iterative depth-first traversal, retaining one shared visited array.
options.feedback: Each traversal marks exactly one whole group. The outer scan also includes isolated vertices, and shared marks prevent counting a group twice.

options.text: Scan every vertex with one shared visited array. Start a breadth-first traversal at each unvisited vertex and count how many traversals are started.
options.feedback: Changing the frontier from a stack to a queue does not change group membership. This explores every group once with the same resource bounds.

options.text: Build a full boolean adjacency matrix, then scan vertices and traverse unvisited groups by inspecting full matrix rows.
options.feedback: This finds the right groups for every input, but allocates and scans absent links as well. The supplied lists already expose exactly the neighbors needed; matrix conversion adds removable work and storage on sparse inputs.

options.text: Count the vertices whose adjacency lists are nonempty.
options.feedback: For lists=[[1],[0],[]], this returns 2, which happens to match, but for [[1],[0]] it returns 2 instead of 1. A vertex with neighbors is not a separate group, and isolated vertices must also be counted.

feedback.reason: A shared visited state partitions the entire graph into reachable groups; a traversal from only one seed would miss disconnected groups.
details: Initialize a boolean visited array to false. Scan vertex IDs in order. For each unvisited ID, increase the group count, mark it and push it onto an explicit stack. Pop vertices and scan their adjacency lists, marking each unseen neighbor before pushing it. Finish that stack before continuing the outer scan. Return the count.
Start a traversal at every still-unvisited vertex, including an isolated one. Each start identifies one new connected component. Starting only at a chosen worker would miss disconnected groups.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze dfs-forest exactly as revealed. V counts all vertices, including isolates; E counts undirected edges, each stored twice. Include initialization of the visited array and the outer scan. Use a preallocated stack of capacity V with constant-time push/pop and array indexing. No hashing, recursion, input copying, or adjacency-list copying is used. Exclude the supplied lists and scalar output; include all working storage.
constraints: Choose the tightest standard worst-case bound for the specified implementation.

options.text: O(V + E) time, O(V) auxiliary space
O(V + E) time, O(1) auxiliary space
O(V² + E) time, O(V²) auxiliary space

feedback.reason: A DFS forest visits each vertex and each undirected adjacency entry once.
details: The option “O(V + E) time, O(V) auxiliary space” is tight: initialize and scan V entries, push each vertex once, and inspect 2E adjacency entries in total. The visited array and explicit stack use O(V) space. The option “O(V + E) time, O(1) auxiliary space” omits both working structures. The option “O(V² + E) time, O(V²) auxiliary space” describes scanning a matrix rather than the supplied lists. The option “O(VE) time, O(V) auxiliary space” incorrectly charges the entire edge set once per vertex; shared marks avoid that repeated exploration.
